claim: The lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the surface-exposed leaflet of the outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the surface-exposed leaflet of the outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria, an organelle that shields the underlying peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell envelope structure.

claim: The outer membrane shields the underlying peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall.
source: The lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the surface-exposed leaflet of the outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria, an organelle that shields the underlying peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell envelope structure.

claim: Both LPS and PG are essential cell envelope components.
source: Both LPS and PG are essential cell envelope components that are synthesized independently and assembled by dedicated transenvelope multiprotein complexes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell envelope components.

claim: LPS and PG are synthesized independently.
source: Both LPS and PG are essential cell envelope components that are synthesized independently and assembled by dedicated transenvelope multiprotein complexes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial biosynthetic pathways.

claim: LPS and PG are assembled by dedicated transenvelope multiprotein complexes.
source: Both LPS and PG are essential cell envelope components that are synthesized independently and assembled by dedicated transenvelope multiprotein complexes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial assembly machinery.

claim: A point-mutation in the gene for O-antigen ligase (WaaL) in Escherichia coli causes LPS to be modified with PG subunits.
source: We have identified a point-mutation in the gene for O-antigen ligase (WaaL) in Escherichia coli that causes LPS to be modified with PG subunits, intersecting these two pathways.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including LPS silver staining, mass spectrometry, and mutanolysin digestion experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The point-mutation in WaaL intersects the LPS and PG biosynthetic pathways.
source: We have identified a point-mutation in the gene for O-antigen ligase (WaaL) in Escherichia coli that causes LPS to be modified with PG subunits, intersecting these two pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 uses lipid II (a PG precursor) to modify LPS.

claim: Synthesis of the PG-modified LPS (LPS*) requires ready access to the small PG precursor pool.
source: Synthesis of the PG-modified LPS (LPS*) requires ready access to the small PG precursor pool but does not weaken cell wall integrity, challenging models of precursor sequestration at PG assembly machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 efficiently modifies approximately one-third of LPS molecules with lipid II-derived DPP despite the scarcity of lipid II.

claim: Synthesis of LPS* does not weaken cell wall integrity.
source: Synthesis of the PG-modified LPS (LPS*) requires ready access to the small PG precursor pool but does not weaken cell wall integrity, challenging models of precursor sequestration at PG assembly machinery.
evidence: This is supported by LC/MS analysis of peptidoglycan showing nearly identical composition between waaL+ and waaL15 strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The observation that LPS* synthesis does not weaken cell wall integrity challenges models of precursor sequestration at PG assembly machinery.
source: Synthesis of the PG-modified LPS (LPS*) requires ready access to the small PG precursor pool but does not weaken cell wall integrity, challenging models of precursor sequestration at PG assembly machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that WaaL15 has ready access to lipid II without compromising cell wall integrity.

claim: LPS* is efficiently transported to the cell surface.
source: LPS* is efficiently transported to the cell surface without impairing OM function.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy showing vancomycin-BODIPY labeling at the cell surface (Figure 4B) and the observation that waaL15 does not cause OM defects.

claim: LPS* transport to the cell surface does not impair OM function.
source: LPS* is efficiently transported to the cell surface without impairing OM function.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that waaL15 does not increase sensitivity to other antibiotics (Figure 1B), indicating the OM barrier remains intact.

claim: LPS* contains the canonical vancomycin binding site.
source: Because LPS* contains the canonical vancomycin binding site, these surface-exposed molecules confer increased vancomycin-resistance by functioning as molecular decoys that titrate the antibiotic away from its intracellular target.
evidence: This is supported by surface plasmon resonance data showing LPS* binds vancomycin with Kd = 0.48 ± 0.08 µM (Figure 4A) and mass spectrometry showing LPS* contains D-Ala-D-Ala residues (Figure 3C).

claim: Surface-exposed LPS* molecules confer increased vancomycin-resistance.
source: Because LPS* contains the canonical vancomycin binding site, these surface-exposed molecules confer increased vancomycin-resistance by functioning as molecular decoys that titrate the antibiotic away from its intracellular target.
evidence: This is supported by vancomycin resistance assays showing waaL15 strains have increased resistance (Figure 1A) and fluorescence microscopy showing vancomycin binding at the cell surface (Figure 4B).

claim: LPS* confers vancomycin resistance by functioning as molecular decoys that titrate the antibiotic away from its intracellular target.
source: Because LPS* contains the canonical vancomycin binding site, these surface-exposed molecules confer increased vancomycin-resistance by functioning as molecular decoys that titrate the antibiotic away from its intracellular target.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of observations: LPS* binds vancomycin at the cell surface, contains D-Ala-D-Ala residues, and correlates with increased vancomycin resistance.

claim: LPS* glycosylation fuses two potent pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
source: This unexpected LPS glycosylation fuses two potent pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge that both LPS and PG are PAMPs, combined with the experimental finding that LPS is modified with PG subunits.

claim: A peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is an essential extracytoplasmic feature of most bacteria.
source: A peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is an essential extracytoplasmic feature of most bacteria (Singer et al., 1989); this essentiality has made its biogenesis a fruitful target for antibiotics, including vancomycin and penicillin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Singer et al., 1989.

claim: The essentiality of the PG cell wall has made its biogenesis a fruitful target for antibiotics, including vancomycin and penicillin.
source: A peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is an essential extracytoplasmic feature of most bacteria (Singer et al., 1989); this essentiality has made its biogenesis a fruitful target for antibiotics, including vancomycin and penicillin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antibiotic mechanisms.

claim: The cell wall is directly exposed to the extracellular milieu in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: The cell wall is directly exposed to the extracellular milieu in Gram-positive bacteria, but is shielded in Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative species by a highly selective permeability barrier formed by the outer membrane (OM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell envelope structure.

claim: The cell wall is shielded in Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative species by a highly selective permeability barrier formed by the outer membrane (OM).
source: The cell wall is directly exposed to the extracellular milieu in Gram-positive bacteria, but is shielded in Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative species by a highly selective permeability barrier formed by the outer membrane (OM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gram-negative bacterial cell envelope structure.

claim: The OM prevents influx of antibiotics, such as vancomycin, restricting their access to intracellular targets.
source: The OM prevents influx of antibiotics, such as vancomycin, restricting their access to intracellular targets (Eggert et al., 2001; Ruiz et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eggert et al., 2001 and Ruiz et al., 2005.

claim: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the surface-exposed outer leaflet of the OM and is key to the barrier function.
source: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) forms the surface-exposed outer leaflet of the OM and is key to the barrier function (Osborn et al., 1972; Kamio and Nikaido, 1976; Nikaido, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Osborn et al., 1972; Kamio and Nikaido, 1976; and Nikaido, 2003.

claim: LPS is a glycolipid consisting of a 'lipid A' anchor within the bilayer, and a set of covalently attached distal 'core' saccharides.
source: LPS is a glycolipid consisting of a 'lipid A' anchor within the bilayer, and a set of covalently attached distal 'core' saccharides (Raetz and Whitfield, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Raetz and Whitfield, 2002.

claim: LPS is made at the cytosolic leaflet of the inner membrane (IM) before being flipped to the periplasmic leaflet.
source: LPS is made at the cytosolic leaflet of the inner membrane (IM) before being flipped to the periplasmic leaflet (Zhou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 1998.

claim: A transenvelope complex of seven lipopolysaccharide transport proteins (LptABCDEFG) delivers LPS from the IM to the OM.
source: A transenvelope complex of seven lipopolysaccharide transport proteins (LptABCDEFG) delivers LPS from the IM to the OM (Ruiz et al., 2009; Chng et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ruiz et al., 2009 and Chng et al., 2010a.

claim: A sub-complex of the β-barrel LptD and lipoprotein LptE resides within the OM and accomplishes the final step of inserting LPS into the outer leaflet.
source: A sub-complex of the β-barrel LptD and lipoprotein LptE resides within the OM and accomplishes the final step of inserting LPS into the outer leaflet (Chng et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chng et al., 2010b.

claim: The lptE613 mutation causes defective LPS transport and leads to increased antibiotic sensitivity.
source: A recently described lptE mutation (lptE613) causes defective LPS transport and leads to increased antibiotic sensitivity (Malojčić et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malojčić et al., 2014.

claim: Spontaneous suppressors that restored antibiotic resistance were isolated to better understand the basis of the lptE613 defect.
source: To better understand the basis of the lptE613 defect, we isolated spontaneous suppressors that restored antibiotic resistance.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: One vancomycin-resistant suppressor mapped to the waaL gene.
source: One such vancomycin-resistant suppressor mapped to the waaL gene, the product of which is an IM glycosyltransferase that attaches O-antigen (O-Ag) oligosaccharides to LPS (Han et al., 2012; Ruan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from linkage mapping described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: WaaL is an IM glycosyltransferase that attaches O-antigen (O-Ag) oligosaccharides to LPS.
source: One such vancomycin-resistant suppressor mapped to the waaL gene, the product of which is an IM glycosyltransferase that attaches O-antigen (O-Ag) oligosaccharides to LPS (Han et al., 2012; Ruan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2012 and Ruan et al., 2012.

claim: The suppressed strain is no more vancomycin sensitive than the corresponding wild-type control.
source: Indeed, the suppressed strain is certainly no more vancomycin sensitive than is the corresponding wild-type control (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by vancomycin resistance assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The waaL15 suppressor was not specific for lptE613 or for LPS transport defects.
source: However, this suppressor (waaL15 herein) was not specific for lptE613 or even for LPS transport defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that waaL15 increases vancomycin resistance in multiple different strain backgrounds including bamB and bamE mutants (Figure 1).

claim: The waaL15 mutation increases vancomycin resistance in strains carrying bamB or bamE null mutations that disrupt the OM barrier by causing defects in β-barrel protein assembly.
source: The waaL15 mutation increases vancomycin resistance in strains carrying bamB or bamE null mutations that disrupt the OM barrier by causing defects in β-barrel protein assembly (Figure 1B) (Ricci and Silhavy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by vancomycin resistance assay data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Ricci and Silhavy, 2012.

claim: waaL15 increases vancomycin-resistance even in the wild-type strain.
source: Moreover, waaL15 also increases vancomycin-resistance even in the wild-type strain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by vancomycin resistance assay data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The waaL15 suppressor does not qualitatively improve the OM barrier.
source: The suppressor does not qualitatively improve the OM barrier, since it did not increase resistance against other antibiotics (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic disc diffusion assay data shown in Figure 1B showing no increased resistance to erythromycin or rifampin.

claim: waaL15 provides a vancomycin-specific resistance mechanism across different strains.
source: So, waaL15 provides a vancomycin-specific resistance mechanism across different strains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations that waaL15 increases vancomycin resistance in multiple strain backgrounds but does not increase resistance to other antibiotics.

claim: The domesticated E. coli K-12 does not produce the normal substrate (O-Ag) of WaaL.
source: The domesticated E. coli K-12 does not produce the normal substrate (O-Ag) of WaaL (Liu and Reeves, 1994) and a waaL deletion does not suppress vancomycin sensitivity, indicating that waaL15 is a gain-of-function mutation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu and Reeves, 1994.

claim: A waaL deletion does not suppress vancomycin sensitivity.
source: The domesticated E. coli K-12 does not produce the normal substrate (O-Ag) of WaaL (Liu and Reeves, 1994) and a waaL deletion does not suppress vancomycin sensitivity, indicating that waaL15 is a gain-of-function mutation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation that supports the conclusion that waaL15 is a gain-of-function mutation.

claim: waaL15 is a gain-of-function mutation.
source: The domesticated E. coli K-12 does not produce the normal substrate (O-Ag) of WaaL (Liu and Reeves, 1994) and a waaL deletion does not suppress vancomycin sensitivity, indicating that waaL15 is a gain-of-function mutation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that waaL deletion does not suppress vancomycin sensitivity while waaL15 does.

claim: The WaaL15 mutant O-Ag ligase contains an F332S substitution.
source: Thus, the WaaL15 mutant O-Ag ligase, which contains an F332S substitution, must have an altered activity.
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing data described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The WaaL15 mutant O-Ag ligase has an altered activity.
source: Thus, the WaaL15 mutant O-Ag ligase, which contains an F332S substitution, must have an altered activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 produces a new LPS glycoform and confers vancomycin resistance.

claim: WaaL15 modifies LPS with additional sugars to produce an additional glycoform (LPS*).
source: Silver-staining of isolated LPS confirmed that WaaL15 modifies LPS with additional sugars to produce an additional glycoform (LPS*), detected as a higher molecular-weight band that is absent in waaL+ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LPS silver staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LPS* is detected as a higher molecular-weight band that is absent in waaL+.
source: Silver-staining of isolated LPS confirmed that WaaL15 modifies LPS with additional sugars to produce an additional glycoform (LPS*), detected as a higher molecular-weight band that is absent in waaL+ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LPS silver staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: WaaL can use two minor saccharide substrates to modify LPS in E. coli K-12: enterobacterial common-antigen (ECA) and colanic acid (CA).
source: WaaL can use two minor saccharide substrates to modify LPS in E. coli K-12: enterobacterial common-antigen (ECA) and colanic acid (CA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about WaaL substrate specificity.

claim: ECA-modified LPS is a minor constituent of the OM.
source: ECA-modified LPS is a minor constituent of the OM (Schmidt et al., 1976; Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 1976 and Meredith et al., 2007.

claim: Production of CA is regulated by the Rcs phospho-relay stress response system.
source: Production of CA is regulated by the Rcs phospho-relay stress response system, and CA-modified LPS (called 'M-LPS') is only detectable during severe envelope stress (Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meredith et al., 2007.

claim: CA-modified LPS (called 'M-LPS') is only detectable during severe envelope stress.
source: Production of CA is regulated by the Rcs phospho-relay stress response system, and CA-modified LPS (called 'M-LPS') is only detectable during severe envelope stress (Meredith et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meredith et al., 2007.

claim: LPS* remained detectable when biosynthesis of ECA (rff), CA (cpsG), or both these polysaccharides (rff cpsG) was inactivated.
source: However, LPS silver-staining revealed that LPS* remained detectable when we inactivated biosynthesis of ECA (rff), CA (cpsG), or both these polysaccharides (rff cpsG) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by LPS silver staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Introducing the rcsC137 mutation to activate expression of the genes for CA biosynthesis results in lowered LPS* abundance at the expense of increased M-LPS.
source: Moreover, if we increase the amounts of a competing substrate by introducing the rcsC137 mutation to activate expression of the genes for CA biosynthesis (Gottesman et al., 1985), we actually observed lowered LPS* abundance at the expense of increased M-LPS (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by LPS silver staining data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Gottesman et al., 1985.

claim: The decrease in LPS* correlated with a significant reduction in vancomycin-resistance.
source: Notably, the decrease in LPS* correlated with a significant reduction in vancomycin-resistance, providing evidence that LPS* molecules directly mediate the resistance (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by vancomycin resistance assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LPS* molecules directly mediate vancomycin resistance.
source: Notably, the decrease in LPS* correlated with a significant reduction in vancomycin-resistance, providing evidence that LPS* molecules directly mediate the resistance (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between LPS* abundance and vancomycin resistance levels.

claim: Restoring O-antigen biosynthesis by introducing a wild-type wbbL gene results in lowered LPS* at the expense of wild-type LPS and reduced vancomycin resistance.
source: Similarly, if O-antigen biosynthesis is restored by introducing a wild-type wbbL gene, we observe lowered LPS* at the expense of wild-type LPS and vancomycin resistance is reduced.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supporting the conclusion that LPS* mediates vancomycin resistance.

claim: WaaL15 is able to use a new substrate and thereby generate a previously uncharacterized LPS glycoform that provides a specific mechanism for vancomycin resistance.
source: We conclude that WaaL15 is able to use a new substrate and thereby generate a previously uncharacterized LPS glycoform that provides a specific mechanism for vancomycin resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including LPS silver staining, mass spectrometry, and vancomycin resistance assays.

claim: All native WaaL substrates contain carbohydrates linked to a common undecaprenyl (Und) lipid carrier.
source: All native WaaL substrates contain carbohydrates linked to a common undecaprenyl (Und) lipid carrier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about WaaL substrate structure.

claim: PG biosynthesis involves a disaccharide pentapeptide (DPP) linked to the same Und carrier, a molecule called lipid II.
source: PG biosynthesis involves a disaccharide pentapeptide (DPP) linked to the same Und carrier, a molecule called lipid II (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan biosynthesis, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Digestion of purified LPS* with mutanolysin liberated near-stoichiometric quantities of fragments that were identified by mass spectrometry as DPP or derivatives with a tetrapeptide stem.
source: Digestion of purified LPS*, but not LPS, liberated near-stoichiometric quantities of fragments that were identified by mass spectrometry as DPP or derivatives with a tetrapeptide stem (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no evidence for cross-linked products suggesting that lipid II was the source of the LPS* glycosylation.
source: Importantly, there is no evidence for cross-linked products suggesting that lipid II was the source of the LPS* glycosylation (Lebar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis and citation to Lebar et al., 2013.

claim: There are several carboxypeptidases in the periplasm that remove the terminal D-Alanine (D-Ala) from DPP to produce the tetrapeptide derivative.
source: There are several carboxypeptidases in the periplasm that remove the terminal D-Alanine (D-Ala) from DPP to produce the tetrapeptide derivative.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan processing enzymes.

claim: E. coli PG contains negligible amounts of pentapeptide stems.
source: Indeed, E. coli PG contains negligible amounts of pentapeptide stems (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis of peptidoglycan shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: About 50% of the LPS* is sequestered before it can be attacked by one of the carboxypeptidases.
source: Figure 3C shows that about 50% of the LPS* is sequestered before it can be attacked by one of these carboxypeptidases.
evidence: This is inferred from the LC-MS data in Figure 3C showing approximately equal amounts of pentapeptide and tetrapeptide forms.

claim: Sequestration of LPS* happens because the molecule is transported from the periplasm to the cell surface.
source: It seemed likely that sequestration happens because the molecule is transported from the periplasm to the cell surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that about 50% of LPS* retains pentapeptide stems and the knowledge that LPS is transported to the cell surface.

claim: Peptide stems from adjacent peptidoglycan strands in the cell wall are cross-linked via transpeptidation between the penultimate D-Ala on one stem and a meso-diaminopimelic acid (m-DAP) residue on a nearby stem.
source: Peptide stems from adjacent peptidoglycan strands in the cell wall are cross-linked via transpeptidation between the penultimate D-Ala on one stem and a meso-diaminopimelic acid (m-DAP) residue on a nearby stem (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: Extensive cross-linking produces a rigid macromolecular meshwork that is vital to cell wall function.
source: Extensive cross-linking produces a rigid macromolecular meshwork that is vital to cell wall function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure and function.

claim: Vancomycin binds and sequesters the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala residues of a pentapeptide stem in order to inhibit transpeptidation.
source: Vancomycin binds and sequesters the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala residues of a pentapeptide stem in order to inhibit transpeptidation (Perkins, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perkins, 1969.

claim: LPS* was immobilized on a carboxymethylated dextran (CM3) chip and surface plasmon resonance was used to monitor interactions with differing concentrations of vancomycin.
source: LPS* was immobilized on a carboxymethylated dextran (CM3) chip and we used surface plasmon resonance to monitor interactions with differing concentrations of vancomycin.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Specific binding of vancomycin to LPS* was measured with a Kd = 0.48 ± 0.08 µM.
source: We were able to measure specific binding of vancomycin to LPS* and to obtain a Kd = 0.48 ± 0.08 µM (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is comparable to a reported Kd for vancomycin-lipid II interactions in vesicles (Al-Kaddah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by surface plasmon resonance data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Kd for vancomycin-LPS* binding is comparable to a reported Kd for vancomycin-lipid II interactions in vesicles.
source: We were able to measure specific binding of vancomycin to LPS* and to obtain a Kd = 0.48 ± 0.08 µM (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is comparable to a reported Kd for vancomycin-lipid II interactions in vesicles (Al-Kaddah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to data cited from Al-Kaddah et al., 2010.

claim: LPS* molecules include high affinity binding sites for vancomycin.
source: Clearly, LPS* molecules include high affinity binding sites for vancomycin.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured Kd of 0.48 µM for vancomycin-LPS* binding.

claim: Live cell microscopy was performed using a fluorescent vancomycin-BODIPY.
source: To test this hypothesis, we performed live cell microscopy using a fluorescent vancomycin-BODIPY.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A wild-type strain background with an intact OM prevents the influx of vancomycin, avoiding labeling intracellular sites of PG synthesis.
source: We used a wild-type strain background with an intact OM that prevents the influx of vancomycin, to avoid labeling intracellular sites of PG synthesis.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: waaL+ cells could not be fluorescently labeled with vancomycin-BODIPY.
source: Indeed, waaL+ cells could not be fluorescently labeled (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Circumferential labeling of waaL15 bacteria was readily detected, confirming the presence of accessible D-Ala-D-Ala residues at the cell surface.
source: On the other hand, we readily detected circumferential labeling of waaL15 bacteria, confirming the presence of accessible D-Ala-D-Ala residues at the cell surface (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Several vancomycin-resistance mechanisms exist in Gram-positive bacteria, including alterations in peptidoglycan metabolism that produce thicker cell walls.
source: Several vancomycin-resistance mechanisms exist in Gram-positive bacteria, including: alterations in peptidoglycan metabolism can produce thicker cell walls (Cui et al., 2003); and transpeptidation can be reduced to leave more free D-Ala-D-Ala residues within the established cell wall structure (Sieradzki and Tomasz, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cui et al., 2003.

claim: Transpeptidation can be reduced to leave more free D-Ala-D-Ala residues within the established cell wall structure as a vancomycin-resistance mechanism in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Several vancomycin-resistance mechanisms exist in Gram-positive bacteria, including: alterations in peptidoglycan metabolism can produce thicker cell walls (Cui et al., 2003); and transpeptidation can be reduced to leave more free D-Ala-D-Ala residues within the established cell wall structure (Sieradzki and Tomasz, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sieradzki and Tomasz, 1997.

claim: Virtually all of the terminal D-Ala residues of DPP are removed either by cross-linking or by the carboxypeptidases in E. coli.
source: It was not immediately apparent to us that any of these strategies could be employed in E. coli since virtually all of the terminal D-Ala residues of DPP are removed either by cross-linking or by the carboxypeptidases.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about E. coli peptidoglycan processing.

claim: The waaL15 mechanism is comparable to Gram-positive vancomycin resistance mechanisms since it also increases the number of free D-Ala-D-Ala targets that can tie up vancomycin.
source: However, we show that the waaL15 mechanism is comparable since it also increases the number of free D-Ala-D-Ala targets that can tie up vancomycin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LPS* contains D-Ala-D-Ala residues that bind vancomycin.

claim: By displaying D-Ala-D-Ala at the cell surface the waaL15 mutation titrates vancomycin away from the true drug target, in an altogether different cellular compartment.
source: Moreover, by displaying D-Ala-D-Ala at the cell surface the waaL15 mutation titrates vancomycin away from the true drug target, in an altogether different cellular compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vancomycin binds to LPS* at the cell surface while its target is in the periplasm.

claim: LPS* confers resistance by acting as a molecular decoy for vancomycin.
source: Therefore, LPS* confers resistance by acting as a molecular decoy for vancomycin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations including vancomycin binding at the cell surface and increased resistance.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria are inherently resistant to vancomycin.
source: Given that Gram-negative bacteria are inherently resistant to vancomycin this decoy mechanism may not be of clinical significance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Gram-negative bacterial antibiotic resistance.

claim: The decoy mechanism may not be of clinical significance.
source: Given that Gram-negative bacteria are inherently resistant to vancomycin this decoy mechanism may not be of clinical significance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the inherent vancomycin resistance of Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: The increased resistance conferred by waaL15 demonstrates the tremendous adaptability of bacteria under antibiotic stress.
source: However, the increased resistance it does confer clearly demonstrates the tremendous adaptability of bacteria under antibiotic stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of bacterial evolution.

claim: Lipid II in E. coli is extremely scarce, its steady-state abundance is thought to be only 1000–2000 molecules per cell.
source: Lipid II in E. coli is extremely scarce, its steady-state abundance is thought to be only 1000–2000 molecules per cell (van Heijenoort et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Heijenoort et al., 1992.

claim: Insertion of new PG is thought to occur via large multiprotein morphogenic complexes: the elongasome and the divisome, responsible for PG synthesis along the lateral cell body and at the septum, respectively.
source: Insertion of new PG is thought to occur via large multiprotein morphogenic complexes: the elongasome and the divisome, responsible for PG synthesis along the lateral cell body and at the septum, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan synthesis machinery.

claim: Both the elongasome and divisome complexes are suggested to include at least some of the lipid II biosynthetic enzymes, and the presumed flippases that deliver lipid II from the site of synthesis in the cytoplasm to the site of cell wall assembly in the periplasm.
source: In order to overcome the scarcity of lipid II and limit its diffusion away from sites of PG growth, both complexes are suggested to include at least some of the lipid II biosynthetic enzymes, and the presumed flippases that deliver lipid II from the site of synthesis in the cytoplasm to the site of cell wall assembly in the periplasm (Szwedziak and Löwe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szwedziak and Löwe, 2013.

claim: In the model of sequestered lipid II, the substrate for PG synthesis would be isolated physically from the LPS assembly pathway.
source: In this model, the substrate for PG synthesis would be isolated physically from the LPS assembly pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the model of lipid II sequestration at PG synthesis complexes.

claim: LPS is inserted into the OM of each cell at a rate exceeding 70,000 molecules per minute.
source: LPS is inserted into the OM of each cell at a rate exceeding 70,000 molecules per minute (Lima et al., 2013) and we approximate that one-third of LPS is modified by WaaL15 with lipid II-sourced DPP.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lima et al., 2013.

claim: Approximately one-third of LPS is modified by WaaL15 with lipid II-sourced DPP.
source: LPS is inserted into the OM of each cell at a rate exceeding 70,000 molecules per minute (Lima et al., 2013) and we approximate that one-third of LPS is modified by WaaL15 with lipid II-sourced DPP.
evidence: This is based on quantification of LPS* band density described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: WaaL15 has ready access to lipid II.
source: Clearly, WaaL15 has ready access to lipid II and this is inconsistent with a model of diffusion-limited lipid II sequestered at the elongasome or divisome complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 efficiently modifies approximately one-third of LPS molecules with lipid II-derived DPP.

claim: WaaL15's ready access to lipid II is inconsistent with a model of diffusion-limited lipid II sequestered at the elongasome or divisome complexes.
source: Clearly, WaaL15 has ready access to lipid II and this is inconsistent with a model of diffusion-limited lipid II sequestered at the elongasome or divisome complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that WaaL15 has ready access to lipid II.

claim: Recent evidence points to wider lipid II availability.
source: Recent evidence also points to wider lipid II availability (Lee et al., 2014; Sham et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Sham et al., 2014.

claim: The re-charging of the lipid carrier with new DPP must be extremely efficient to maintain such a robust pool of PG precursor.
source: Our data indicate that the re-charging of the lipid carrier with new DPP must also be extremely efficient to maintain such a robust pool of PG precursor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 can efficiently modify LPS with lipid II-derived DPP without depleting the pool needed for cell wall synthesis.

claim: WaaL15 drains the available lipid II pool with no apparent detriment to cell wall integrity.
source: WaaL15 drains the available lipid II pool with no apparent detriment to cell wall integrity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis of peptidoglycan showing nearly identical composition between waaL+ and waaL15 strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Lipid II limitation can be revealed by synthetic genetic interactions in a strain lacking the elongasome.
source: Lipid II limitation can be revealed by synthetic genetic interactions in a strain lacking the elongasome (Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014), but it is not the recharging of lipid II that is limiting, rather it is the biosynthesis of DPP (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014 and genetic interaction data in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: It is not the recharging of lipid II that is limiting, rather it is the biosynthesis of DPP.
source: Lipid II limitation can be revealed by synthetic genetic interactions in a strain lacking the elongasome (Paradis-Bleau et al., 2014), but it is not the recharging of lipid II that is limiting, rather it is the biosynthesis of DPP (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data showing that overexpression of murA (which increases DPP biosynthesis) relieves the synthetic interaction (Supplementary file 1A).

claim: In many bacteria, LPS is decorated with highly variable O-Ags that are linear polymers of repeating units of 3–6 monosaccharides.
source: In many bacteria, LPS is decorated with highly variable O-Ags that are linear polymers of repeating units of 3–6 monosaccharides (Kalynych et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kalynych et al., 2014.

claim: In E. coli the multitude of different O-Ags initiate with GlcNAc.
source: In E. coli the multitude of different O-Ags initiate with GlcNAc, ECA also initiates with GlcNAc.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli O-antigen and ECA structure.

claim: ECA initiates with GlcNAc.
source: In E. coli the multitude of different O-Ags initiate with GlcNAc, ECA also initiates with GlcNAc.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ECA structure.

claim: In E. coli K-12 when colanic acid is overproduced M-LPS is made from an initiating Glc residue.
source: In E. coli K-12 when colonic acid is overproduced M-LPS is made from an intitating Glc residue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about colanic acid-modified LPS structure.

claim: The F332S mutation broadens substrate specificity of the WaaL glycosyltransferase allowing it to efficiently accept a significantly more bulky initiating MurNAc with an attached oligopeptide stem.
source: The F332S mutation broadens substrate specificity of the WaaL glycosyltransferase allowing it to efficiently accept a significantly more bulky initiating MurNAc with an attached oligopeptide stem.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that WaaL15 (containing F332S) can use lipid II as a substrate while wild-type WaaL cannot.

claim: The only other glycosyltransferase that is known to use lipid II as a substrate is PglL from Neisseria and the use required overproduction of the enzyme in E. coli.
source: The only other glycosyltransferase that is known to use lipid II as a substrate is PglL from Neisseria and the use required overproduction of the enzyme in E. coli (Faridmoayer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Faridmoayer et al., 2008.

claim: No OM biogenesis defect is detected in strains carrying waaL15.
source: It is also remarkable that we detect no OM biogenesis defect in strains carrying waaL15, demonstrating that the Lpt system is fully competent for the transport and assembly of LPS* despite the addition of both unnatural sugars and peptide stems.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that waaL15 does not increase sensitivity to other antibiotics (Figure 1B).

claim: The Lpt system is fully competent for the transport and assembly of LPS* despite the addition of both unnatural sugars and peptide stems.
source: It is also remarkable that we detect no OM biogenesis defect in strains carrying waaL15, demonstrating that the Lpt system is fully competent for the transport and assembly of LPS* despite the addition of both unnatural sugars and peptide stems.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that waaL15 strains do not show OM defects despite producing LPS*.

claim: Both LPS and PG are pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that potently activate innate immune responses via distinct pathways.
source: Both LPS and PG are pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that potently activate innate immune responses via distinct pathways, and it seems sensible for Gram-negative bacteria to keep these entities separated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about innate immune recognition of bacterial components.

claim: It seems sensible for Gram-negative bacteria to keep LPS and PG separated.
source: Both LPS and PG are pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that potently activate innate immune responses via distinct pathways, and it seems sensible for Gram-negative bacteria to keep these entities separated.
evidence: This is speculation based on the knowledge that LPS and PG are distinct PAMPs.

claim: The F332S substitution has inactivated an exclusion mechanism that prevents WaaL from utilizing the lipid II pool.
source: We suggest that the F332S substitution has inactivated an exclusion mechanism that prevents WaaL from utilizing the lipid II pool.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that WaaL15 can use lipid II while wild-type WaaL cannot.

claim: LPS* constitutes 29 ± 1% of the total LPS in waaL15 samples.
source: By quantifying band density using ImageJ, we measured that LPS* constitutes 29 ± 1% of the total LPS in waaL15 samples.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of LPS silver staining data.

claim: The waaL15 mutation was isolated as a spontaneous suppressor of strain MG1029 capable of growing on LB plates supplemented with vancomycin (140 μg/ml).
source: Spontaneous suppressor mutants of strain MG1029 capable of growing on LB plates supplemented with vancomycin (140 μg/ml) were isolated; one such mutant strain was MG1088.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for isolating the waaL15 mutation.

claim: The mutation locus conferring vancomycin-resistance in MG1088 was identified by linkage mapping using a library of random mini-Tn10 insertions.
source: The mutation locus conferring vancomycin-resistance in MG1088 was identified by linkage mapping using a library of random mini-Tn10 insertions (Kleckner et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used and is supported by citation to Kleckner et al., 1991.

claim: The tdh::Tn10 allele was found to be approximately 70% linked to the suppressor mutation waaL15.
source: In this way, the tdh::Tn10 allele was found to be approximately 70% linked to the suppressor mutation waaL15.
evidence: This is supported by linkage mapping data.

claim: The F332S mutation was identified by PCR amplification and sequencing of the waaL locus.
source: The F332S mutation was then identified by PCR amplification and sequencing of the waaL locus.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to identify the specific mutation.

claim: Purified LPS (0.5 mg/ml) from strains MG1210 or MG1211 were extruded in 20 mM Tris/HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl and immobilized on poly-L-lysine coated CM3 Biacore chips.
source: Purified LPS (0.5 mg/ml) from strains MG1210 or MG1211 were extruded in 20 mM Tris/HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl and immobilized on poly-L-lysine coated CM3 Biacore chips on the active and reference channel, respectively (Malojčić et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for surface plasmon resonance analysis and is supported by citation to Malojčić et al., 2014.

claim: All surface plasmon resonance experiments were performed using a Biacore X100 instrument at 25°C at a flow rate of 10 μl/min with 20 mM Tris/HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl buffer.
source: All experiments were performed using a Biacore X100 instrument at 25°C at a flow rate of 10 μl/min with 20 mM Tris/HCl pH 8, 150 mM NaCl buffer.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: Different concentrations of vancomycin were injected for 400 s and dissociation was recorded for another 500 s to return to baseline in the surface plasmon resonance experiments.
source: Different concentrations of vancomycin were injected for 400 s and dissociation was recorded for another 500 s to return to baseline.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: No binding of vancomycin was observed to the reference channel in the surface plasmon resonance experiments.
source: No binding was observed to the reference channel.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supporting the specificity of vancomycin binding to LPS*.

claim: The equilibrium signal in the difference channel was fitted to f = Bmax*abs(x)/(Kd + abs(x)) with R2 = 0.88.
source: The equilibrium signal in the difference channel was fitted to f = Bmax*abs(x)/(Kd + abs(x)) with R2 = 0.88.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method used for surface plasmon resonance experiments.

claim: Standard deviation for vancomycin binding was measured for 0.6 µM and 1.2 µM vancomycin in triplicate and did not exceed 1 RU.
source: Standard deviation was measured for 0.6 µM and 1.2 µM vancomycin in triplicate and did not exceed 1 RU.
evidence: This describes the reproducibility of the surface plasmon resonance measurements.
